coverage.learning_objective: Choose a built-in collection for a storage requirement.

required_facts.statement: A list is a mutable sequence, suitable for ordered positional access with updates.
A tuple is an immutable sequence, suitable for a fixed ordered group of values.
A set stores distinct hashable values without sequence positions and supports membership tests and set operations.
A dictionary maps hashable keys to values, supports updates and preserves insertion order; use it for lookup by key rather than by sequence position.

teaching_blocks.content: Before storing an order-related value, ask what the program will do with it. Positional updates, a fixed pair, distinct membership and key lookup call for different collections.
A list is a mutable sequence, suitable for ordered positional access with updates.

A tuple is an immutable sequence, suitable for a fixed ordered group of values. A set stores distinct hashable values without sequence positions and supports membership tests and set operations. A dictionary maps hashable keys to values, supports updates and preserves insertion order; use it for lookup by key rather than by sequence position.

For example, keep editable quantities in [3, 2, 5], fixed lower and upper bounds in (2, 5), distinct labels in {"notebook", "pen"}, and quantities by label in {"notebook": 3, "pen": 2}. A list allows replacing the item at a position. A tuple keeps a fixed ordered group. A set supports asking whether a label belongs, without a sequence position. A dictionary supports retrieving a quantity by its label and preserves insertion order. Choose by the access and update needed, rather than by which literal is shortest.
Insertion order does not turn a dictionary into a positional sequence. Its lookup is by key. Sets likewise have no sequence positions, even if a particular display looks ordered.

coverage.learning_objective: Account for floating-point approximation in numeric comparisons.

required_facts.statement: Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly as binary floating-point values.
math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=..., abs_tol=...) compares values using relative and absolute tolerances rather than exact equality.
The default relative tolerance is 1e-9 and absolute tolerance is 0.0; comparison to zero requires an appropriate positive absolute tolerance when nonzero differences should count as close.

teaching_blocks.content: Two calculations intended to represent the same decimal amount may differ slightly as floats. State how close is close enough instead of assuming exact equality expresses the requirement.
Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly as binary floating-point values.

math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=..., abs_tol=...) compares values using relative and absolute tolerances rather than exact equality. The default relative tolerance is 1e-9 and absolute tolerance is 0.0; comparison to zero requires an appropriate positive absolute tolerance when nonzero differences should count as close.

Compare using tolerances:
```python
import math
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
print(math.isclose(0.000001, 0.0, abs_tol=0.00001))
```
The results are False, True and True. Many decimal fractions do not have exact binary floating-point representations. The last comparison deliberately allows a small absolute difference near zero. Choose tolerances that match the example's requirement; the defaults are a relative tolerance of 1e-9 and an absolute tolerance of 0.0.
A comparison near zero does not gain a positive absolute allowance from the default abs_tol. Supply an appropriate positive absolute tolerance when a small nonzero difference should count as close.

coverage.learning_objective: Use indentation to express Python block structure.

required_facts.statement: A compound statement’s header ends with a colon and its multi-line suite is an indented block; nested suites require deeper indentation.
Indentation determines statement grouping; dedenting ends a deeper group, and inconsistent indentation can be invalid.
Use four spaces for each indentation level when repairing block structure.

teaching_blocks.content: A loop contains a condition, and a final report belongs after the loop. Indentation is what makes those three levels of grouping visible to Python.
A compound statement’s header ends with a colon and its multi-line suite is an indented block; nested suites require deeper indentation.
Indentation determines statement grouping; dedenting ends a deeper group, and inconsistent indentation can be invalid. Use four spaces for each indentation level when repairing block structure.

Trace the groups in this program:
```python
total = 0
for quantity in [3, -1, 2]:
    if quantity > 0:
        total = total + quantity
print(total)
```
The addition belongs to the if body, which belongs to the for body. The report is dedented to the outer level and displays 5 after the loop. Four spaces mark each level here. Moving the report into the loop would put it in a different group; moving the addition out of the if would remove that condition's grouping around the update.
Indentation is not only a visual preference. It determines grouping, and inconsistent indentation can be invalid. The header ends with a colon; its multi-line body must be indented.

segments.label: Recognise block membership and repair inconsistent indentation
segments.summary: Indentation determines which statements belong to an if body. Statements aligned within that body share its condition; an unindented statement following it is outside the body. The example uses x = 10 and compares x with 5. Giving statements in the same body different indentation produces errors; aligning them consistently repairs the structure. Although consistent two-space indentation can work, use four spaces per level.

segments.label: Build indented bodies and add a deeper nested block
segments.summary: An if header ends with a colon, and its indented statements run only when its condition is true. Moving a following statement into or out of that indentation changes whether it belongs to the conditional body. Inconsistent spacing produces an indentation error. Tabs and spaces are different characters, and mixing them can fail even when their alignment looks similar. Use four spaces per level rather than the alternative widths discussed. An if inside another if introduces a deeper body, indented another four spaces.

bridge_note.after: The first clip does not explain deeper nesting or the colon-ended header requirement; the text covers both. The second demonstrates nested conditions; the text applies the same grouping rules to a condition inside a loop.

coverage.learning_objective: Use range for bounded integer iteration.

required_facts.statement: range(stop) starts at zero with step one; range(start, stop, step) uses the specified start and nonzero step.
The stop value is excluded; a positive step continues below stop and a negative step continues above stop.
Use for index in range(start, stop, 2): to traverse every second integer position in an increasing interval.

teaching_blocks.content: A program needs every second integer position from zero up to a limit. Range expresses the start, excluded stop and step directly.
range(stop) starts at zero with step one; range(start, stop, step) uses the specified start and nonzero step.

The stop value is excluded; a positive step continues below stop and a negative step continues above stop. Use for index in range(start, stop, 2): to traverse every second integer position in an increasing interval.

Compare increasing and decreasing ranges:
```python
for index in range(0, 6, 2):
    print(index)
for index in range(5, 0, -2):
    print(index)
```
The first loop displays 0, 2 and 4; the second displays 5, 3 and 1. In neither case is the stop value included. A positive step continues below the stop, while a negative step continues above it. With range(3), the defaults instead supply zero, one and two. State the step explicitly when the task requires every second integer position.
The stop is excluded, not the last guaranteed value. A negative step also needs a direction compatible with reaching values above its stop, and a step of zero is not allowed.

teaching_blocks.content: The same calculation may appear alone in an interactive session or on the right of an assignment. Distinguish evaluating a value from binding a name to that value.
An expression statement evaluates an expression; in interactive mode its non-None value is displayed.

An assignment evaluates its right-hand expression before binding the resulting value to its target. Python evaluates expressions from left to right; operator precedence and parentheses determine how constituent operations group.

Trace grouping and current values:
```python
quantity = 3
cost = quantity * 4 + 2
quantity = 5
print(cost)
print((quantity + 1) * 4)
```
The displayed results are 14 and 24. The cost assignment evaluates its right side with quantity equal to 3. The later expression uses the now-current quantity of 5, with parentheses grouping its addition. In interactive mode, entering a non-None expression value by itself displays it. Assignment instead evaluates the right-hand expression and binds its result to the target.
Left-to-right evaluation does not erase operator precedence. Use precedence and parentheses to establish grouping while tracing evaluations in their specified order.

A # outside a string starts a comment extending to the physical line’s end; comments are ignored by syntax.

A comment is not evidence that the code implements its description. Read the operation itself, and keep the comment accurate rather than leaving an outdated explanation.

coverage.learning_objective: Explain how Python executes source in a selected runtime.

required_facts.statement: Source can be compiled to a code object; invalid source syntax raises SyntaxError.
In CPython, the compiler produces bytecode used by the interpreter; bytecode is an implementation detail, not a cross-implementation guarantee.
Top-level module statements execute when the module is first imported or when its file is executed as a script.
At runtime, an assignment evaluates its expression using current values and binds the result to its target.

teaching_blocks.content: A saved source file has to be valid before its statements can execute. Keep the source, compilation step and runtime use of values conceptually separate.
Source can be compiled to a code object; invalid source syntax raises SyntaxError.

In CPython, the compiler produces bytecode used by the interpreter; bytecode is an implementation detail, not a cross-implementation guarantee. Top-level module statements execute when the module is first imported or when its file is executed as a script. At runtime, an assignment evaluates its expression using current values and binds the result to its target.

Consider a file containing quantity = 3 followed by cost = quantity * 4. At runtime the first assignment binds quantity to 3, and the second uses that current value to bind cost to 12. Invalid source syntax instead raises SyntaxError when compilation is attempted. In CPython, compilation produces bytecode used by the interpreter. Top-level module statements execute on first import or when the file is run as a script. This model explains where parsing validity and changing runtime bindings fit without requiring you to inspect bytecode instructions.
Bytecode is a CPython implementation detail, not a guarantee about every Python implementation. Do not turn this explanatory model into a universal claim about internal execution machinery.

Expressions inside parentheses, square brackets or braces may span physical lines without backslashes.

Keep the delimiters and expression intact when splitting a long call across lines; continuation indentation does not determine block grouping. Align continuation arguments with the opening delimiter or use a hanging indent.

Keep one expression inside its parentheses:
```python

    3 * 4
    + 2

Parentheses, square brackets and braces allow this kind of implicit continuation without backslashes. Read the opening and closing delimiters before interpreting continuation whitespace as a block boundary.
Continuation indentation is not the rule that groups compound-statement bodies. Preserve delimiters and the expression when splitting a long call; do not mistake it for a newly indented suite.

required_facts.statement: text.strip() returns text with leading and trailing whitespace removed; it does not remove interior whitespace.
The optional chars argument to strip is a set of removable characters, not a literal prefix or suffix.
text.lower() returns a copy with cased characters converted to lowercase.
text.split(separator) separates on that delimiter and preserves empty fields between repeated delimiters.

teaching_blocks.content: Entered labels may contain surrounding spaces and inconsistent letter case. Separate cleanup at the edges from splitting text into fields.
text.strip() returns text with leading and trailing whitespace removed; it does not remove interior whitespace.

The optional chars argument to strip is a set of removable characters, not a literal prefix or suffix. text.lower() returns a copy with cased characters converted to lowercase. text.split(separator) separates on that delimiter and preserves empty fields between repeated delimiters. text.split() without a separator splits on runs of whitespace and omits leading and trailing empty fields.

Compare explicit delimiters with whitespace splitting:
```python
text = "  Blue  "
print(text.strip().lower())
print("red,,blue".split(","))
print("  red   blue  ".split())
print("xylabelyx".strip("xy"))
```
The outputs represent blue, ["red", "", "blue"], ["red", "blue"] and label. The explicit comma preserves an empty field between repeated commas. Whitespace splitting groups runs of whitespace and omits leading and trailing empty fields. In the final call, x and y are removable edge characters, not a required literal prefix or suffix. Interior whitespace is not removed by strip().
strip("xy") does not mean remove exactly one prefix xy and one suffix xy. Its argument describes removable characters at the edges; it is not a literal substring-removal rule.

Syntactically valid code can raise an exception during execution; its error message identifies the exception type and explanation. Invalid syntax prevents the source from compiling to an executable code object, so repair the syntax before tracing that source’s runtime behavior.

required_facts.statement: False, None, numeric zero and empty built-in strings and collections have false truth values; nonzero numbers and nonempty built-in strings and collections have true truth values.

False, None, numeric zero and empty built-in strings and collections have false truth values; nonzero numbers and nonempty built-in strings and collections have true truth values.
Use if collection: for a nonempty guard or if not collection: for an empty guard; truth testing does not require equality to True.

Use the collection itself as the condition:
```python
quantities = []
if not quantities:
    print("No quantities")
quantities = [3]
if quantities:
    print("Quantities available")
```

The same distinction applies to empty and nonempty built-in strings, while zero is false and nonzero numbers are true. False and None are also false in a truth test.
Truth testing does not require collection == True. Use if collection or if not collection for the intended nonempty or empty guard.

None is the singleton object commonly used to represent absence of a value.

is tests whether operands are the same object and is not tests whether they are different objects. Use value is None or value is not None to test absence rather than a truth test that would also reject a legitimate zero or empty value.

Test absence explicitly:
```python
quantity = 0

    print("Quantity supplied", quantity)
quantity = None
if quantity is None:
    print("Quantity absent")
```

In this example the first guard accepts zero because zero is not None. Choose the absence test rather than a broad truth test when zero or an empty value is allowed by the task.
False truth and absence are not interchangeable. A truth test also rejects legitimate zero or empty values; value is None targets the absence marker specifically.

context.concept_name: Encoding and decoding Unicode text and bytes

coverage.learning_objective: Encode and decode between Unicode strings and bytes.

required_facts.statement: str contains Unicode text, distinct from binary bytes.
text.encode("utf-8") produces bytes using UTF-8.
payload.decode("utf-8") produces text from UTF-8 bytes; the decoding encoding must match the encoded data to recover that text.
A decoding failure raises UnicodeDecodeError when the supplied bytes are not valid for the chosen decoding.

teaching_blocks.content: A label is text inside the program but may need an encoded binary payload at a boundary. Keep the text and its encoded bytes as distinct values.
str contains Unicode text, distinct from binary bytes.

text.encode("utf-8") produces bytes using UTF-8. payload.decode("utf-8") produces text from UTF-8 bytes; the decoding encoding must match the encoded data to recover that text. A decoding failure raises UnicodeDecodeError when the supplied bytes are not valid for the chosen decoding.

Encode, then decode with the matching encoding:
```python
text = "café"
payload = text.encode("utf-8")
restored = payload.decode("utf-8")
print(type(text))
print(type(payload))
print(restored)
```
The types are str and bytes, and the restored text is café. Encoding produces bytes from Unicode text; decoding interprets bytes as text under an encoding. A payload whose bytes are invalid for the chosen decoding raises UnicodeDecodeError. Match the decoding encoding to the encoded data rather than treating any bytes value as already-readable text.
bytes and str are not two names for the same kind of value. Recovering the intended text requires a matching decoding encoding, and invalid bytes can cause a decoding failure.
